title: Voice as the Whole Interface
description: Ten audio tools that make speech the input or the product: offline voice assistants, dictation, translation, audiobook conversion and spoken flashcard drills.
content:
# Voice as the Whole Interface

Speech is the oldest interface and the hardest to get right, because a conversation has no undo button and no cursor.

This group of ten splits cleanly. Some tools listen — dictation, transcription, meeting capture. Some speak — audiobooks, drills, phone hosts. And a few do both, which is where it gets interesting.

## Listening properly

[[link:/tools/2282|Sonia]] is the most technically ambitious tool here. It is a local voice assistant that runs entirely on your machine in under 15 GB of RAM with no dedicated GPU, and its headline feature is that the microphone never closes: you can interrupt it mid-sentence and it cancels the rest of the reply while keeping what it already said in history.

The interesting part is how it decides you have finished talking. Microphone audio arrives in 32 ms frames, in-process Silero VAD does the cheap first pass, a Smart Turn classifier decides whether the utterance really ended, and a four-token LISTEN-or-REPLY prompt settles the ambiguous cases. Four mechanisms sounds like overkill until you have used a system that cuts you off mid-thought.

[[link:/tools/2283|SpeakoFlow]] is the pragmatic version: free, open-source dictation into whatever app you are using, in up to 99 languages, with local and cloud models. It also answers questions about selected text, runs a hands-free spoken conversation, and writes up meetings with who said what and a summary — without a bot joining the call.

[[link:/tools/2284|Whistle Translator]] does dictation and translation entirely offline. Eight languages including Arabic, a shortcut that types your words at the cursor in any app, translate-as-you-type, a meeting mode with timestamped transcript, and WAV file transcription. After a one-time model download it works with the Wi-Fi off.

[[link:/tools/2288|TrueScribe]] is the desktop studio version: transcription, timestamped editing, speaker identification with NVIDIA Nemotron, local translation, AI research over the transcript using saved prompts, and export to TXT, SRT, WebVTT, DOCX, PDF, Markdown, JSON and CSV. Windows and Linux, with free transcription.

[[link:/tools/2289|Memorynotch]] puts the recorder in the notch. Record a conversation, follow the live transcript with speaker labels, and keep the audio and notes on your own Mac. Double-tap Command anywhere and a pill appears beside your cursor for dictation, which is free even without a licence.

## Speaking back

[[link:/tools/2285|Book2Speech]] turns a DRM-free EPUB, PDF, TXT, DOCX, MOBI or AZW3 into an audiobook. Drop the file, pick one of 265 narrators across 42 languages, and start listening within seconds, with chapters preserved and front matter skipped. Your place follows you from browser to iPhone.

[[link:/tools/2286|Deckdrill]] turns flashcards into audio drills you can speak along with. Your own AI key writes the Anki cards from a topic and grammar focus, then native neural voices or a clone of your own voice render Pimsleur- and Glossika-style MP3s with pauses timed to each sentence, plus an .apkg with the same audio on every card.

[[link:/tools/2287|Loudwalk]] is the walking version. It asks your Anki cards through your headphones and grades what you say back in your own words — clinical shorthand, a spoken translation, a full rule — because it grades on meaning rather than spelling. Say "tell me more" to open a conversation with an AI teacher, then return to the cards. Screen review is free forever; the voice tutor is $9.99 a month after a trial.

[[link:/tools/2290|ROAL]] is the commercial end. Paste a restaurant website or Maps link and in about two minutes it has a phone host that answers calls, takes pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, quotes a ready time, sends a clean kitchen ticket and hands catering or complaints to a person with a summary. $0.90 per completed order, no monthly fee, and it learns from questions it could not answer.

## The output side

[[link:/tools/2291|Overtone]] is the tooling layer for captions: an open caption format, a video.js plugin with style packs, and a CLI that recuts, burns in and exports word-timed captions. One source file produces captions cut for every screen shape, so vertical and square versions do not need their own transcription pass. It is MIT licensed at 49 stars, early but structurally right.

## What separates the good ones

Two things. First, whether the tool is honest about latency and interruption — [[link:/tools/2282|Sonia]] is the only one here that treats turn-taking as the core problem rather than an afterthought. Second, whether it runs locally. [[link:/tools/2284|Whistle Translator]], [[link:/tools/2289|Memorynotch]] and [[link:/tools/2288|TrueScribe]] all keep audio on the machine, which for a recording of a private conversation is not a feature but a requirement.

The pattern across all ten is that voice tools are judged on what happens at the edges: when you interrupt, when the network drops, when the speaker has an accent, when the call is about an allergen. That is where the engineering shows, and it is where most of these tools have clearly spent their time.
tldr: Sonia, SpeakoFlow, Whistle Translator, Book2Speech, Deckdrill, Loudwalk, TrueScribe, Memorynotch, ROAL and Overtone split between tools that listen to you and tools that speak back.
